title: How to cold email a PI — what actually works
excerpt: Most cold emails to PIs get ignored not because the student isn't good enough, but because the email gives the PI no reason to reply. Here's what I've learned from sending them and reading about what works.
content:
## The honest truth about cold emails

Most PIs receive dozens of cold emails every week. The ones that get replies share one thing: they show the student has actually read the PI's work — not just their lab page headline, but a specific paper, a specific finding, a specific question it left unanswered.

## What to include

**Subject line:** Keep it under 10 words. Include your institution and the specific topic. Example: "BSc Biotech student interested in your m6A methylation work"

**Opening:** Name one specific paper of theirs and say one thing about it that isn't on the abstract. This proves you read it.

**Middle:** Two sentences on who you are, your relevant skills, and what you're hoping to gain. Not your whole CV — just what's relevant to their lab.

**Ask:** Be specific. "Would you be open to a 15-minute call?" is better than "I would love to join your lab."

**Closing:** Attach your CV. Mention you've attached it. Keep the whole email under 200 words.

## What to avoid

- Starting with "I am a highly motivated student" (every email does this)
- Sending the same email to 20 PIs with only the name swapped
- Asking about funding in the first email
- Following up the next day

title: What I wish I knew before my first research internship
excerpt: Starting a lab internship feels exciting until day two when you realize nobody is going to hand you a schedule. Here's what I learned the hard way at IISER Berhampur.
content:
## Nobody tells you this about internships

A research internship is not a course. There is no syllabus, no assignment due on Friday, and no one tracking whether you showed up with energy or dragged yourself in. That freedom is also the trap.

## Lesson 1: Ask questions early, not late

The first week is your window to ask obvious questions without judgment. "How does the autoclave work?" is fine on day three. On day thirty, it's awkward.

## Lesson 2: Keep a lab notebook from day one

Write down what you did, what worked, what didn't, and why you think it didn't. Even if it feels pointless. Especially if it feels pointless. You will reference it more than you expect.

## Lesson 3: Your mentor is busy

They are not ignoring you. They have their own deadlines, their own experiments, their own pressure. Learn to prepare a crisp 2-minute update before you approach them. What did you do, what result did you get, what do you need from them. That's it.

## Lesson 4: Failing an experiment is data

The MTT assay not working taught me more about cell viability troubleshooting than any lecture. Treat failures as protocol. Write them down.

title: GATE BT preparation — how I approached it while in college
excerpt: Qualifying GATE while juggling coursework, internships, and a thesis is doable — but only if you stop treating it like an exam you'll study for later. Here's my honest breakdown.
content:
## The trap most students fall into

GATE preparation gets pushed to "after the semester ends" until suddenly it's January and the exam is in February. I've been there. What changed for me was treating GATE prep as a daily maintenance habit, not a sprint.

## What actually helped

**Concept first, MCQ second.** Doing PYQs before understanding the concept only teaches you to pattern-match the wrong things. GATE BT tests application, not recall.

**Make a subject priority list.** Not all subjects are equal in weightage. Biochemistry, Molecular Biology, and Genetics together make up a disproportionate share of the paper. Start there.

**Use the syllabus as a checklist.** Print it. Cross off topics as you genuinely understand them — not as you "covered" them.

**Mock tests from November.** Full 3-hour mocks under real conditions. Time pressure in GATE is real and it needs practice, not just awareness.

## On balancing it with college

I had thesis work, internship applications, and coursework running simultaneously. The only thing that worked was fixed 1-hour slots before anything else each morning. Not long sessions. Consistent ones.

title: Mastering Molecular Cloning at CSIR-IICB
excerpt: In January 2025, I was selected as 1 of 12 trainees for a skill development program at the Indian Institute of Chemical Biology. Here is what I learned about cloning and protein expression.
content:
## The CSIR-IICB Experience

Getting selected for the "Molecular Cloning, Protein Expression and Structural Characterization" program was a turning point. It bridged the gap between textbook theory and benchwork reality.

## Hands-on Cloning

We cloned our gene of interest into both cloning and expression vectors. The nuances of restriction digestion, ligation, and transformation are much trickier when your hands are doing the pipetting instead of your brain reading a diagram.

## Protein Purification

I was trained in purifying the expressed protein using affinity chromatography and size exclusion chromatography. The satisfaction of seeing a pure protein band on an SDS-PAGE gel is unmatched. We also learned Circular Dichroism and Spectroscopy for structural characterization. 

## Takeaway

If you get a chance to attend a dedicated skill development program, take it. It condenses months of trial-and-error into a few weeks of guided, intensive learning.

title: Navigating International Journal Clubs: STEM for Development
excerpt: I was selected among 30 students globally for the Biomedicine Journal Club. Discussing complex research papers with international peers taught me how to communicate science effectively.
content:
## Why join a journal club?

Reading a paper alone is fine, but dissecting it with 5-6 peers biweekly forces you to confront what you don't understand. Under the guidance of Dr. Schwab and Nicholas Offei, our group tackled complex papers in biomedicine.

## The Papers We Explored

We discussed some fascinating work, including:
- A DNA machine-based magnetic resonance imaging nanoprobe for in vivo microRNA detection.
- Lentiviral vector gene therapy and CFTR modulators in cystic fibrosis rat airway models.

## The Art of Presentation

My biggest takeaway was learning how to present. We focused on effective communication strategies and attention-grabbing visuals to convey key findings. It's not just about reciting data; it's about telling the story of the unknowns and the motivation behind the study.

At the end of the session, I was recognized as one of the most reliable and collaborative members of the club. It reinforced my belief that science is fundamentally a team sport.
